title: Embodiment and Meaning Formation

work.full: Design for Dasein: Understanding the Design of Experiences
work.author: Thomas Wendt

locus_template: (p.N / pdf N)  where N = book page; pdf = book + 2
page_offset_formula: pdf = book_page + 2 (running heads 'Design for Dasein / NN' = book page)
coverage: Embodiment (Merleau-Ponty; anti-Cartesian dualism; machines as simulated organs of the body); embodied cognition and design; how meaning is formed in/through embodied, situated experience; critique of the assumptions that users are rational subjects and that users are conscious of their own goals.
argument_arc: A clearing of three Cartesian assumptions (rational subject; conscious goals; think-then-act) opens an embodiment frame (Merleau-Ponty, Dreyfus, Clark, extended mind) in which what a thing DOES matters more than what it IS; affordances (Gibson via Norman, Tonkinwise, Krippendorff) are the dualism-dissolving hinge; meaning is recast as embodied, distributed, action-contingent, with sense (one context) distinguished from meaning (sum of imaginable contexts); the interface is an active mediation point of structural coupling whose proper design goal is transparency, not invisibility/intuition; the chapter ends opening embodied design practice (semantic turn, systemic turn, situated design, embodied interaction, ethnography). Through-line: from a metaphysics of design to a phenomenology of design.

sections.title: Embodiment
sections.summary: Clears three Cartesian designer-assumptions; introduces embodied cognition (Clark), Dreyfus's Heideggerian critique of symbolic AI, Merleau-Ponty (body as ambiguous third party, skills as solicitations, body as system of possible actions), extended mind, Bonsiepe's structural coupling, and Ihde's amplification/reduction.

sections.title: Affordances and Action
sections.summary: The 'earthy' site of cognition as experience; potentiality bounded by bodily capacity and opened by creative misuse (Franssen, hands); scripts (Latour); affordances (Norman) deepened past communication; Gibson's anti-dualist affordance ('both physical and psychical, yet neither'); Simmel's vase handle; perception vs. capacity to act; the unsemiotic affordance and 'forced abductive thinking' (Tonkinwise); move from metaphysics to phenomenology of design.

sections.title: Embodied Meaning
sections.summary: Embodied meaning arises from acting within the world (brain-in-a-vat has none); action and writing; the Freud analogy; meaning as systemic/contextual; Krippendorff's product semantics (water-bottle example); the sense vs. meaning distinction; use precedes sense; meaning relies on communication and the creative/performative power of language (Wittgenstein via Krippendorff); design as declarative act requiring mediation of communication and usability.

sections.title: Interface
sections.summary: Interface as point of sensemaking and structural coupling (Bonsiepe) and as 'generative friction'; a moving concentration of primary/secondary affordances; contesting Bonsiepe's 'central domain' and the fetishization of the interface; Simon's positivist artifact rejected; Hookway's interface as active mediation yielding a user-system third entity; 'prototypical artifact of the postindustrial era'; critique of intuition/invisibility; transparency vs. invisibility (the central proposal); transparency of use vs. of context; coping and client communication; Ihde's double desire / paradox of invisibility (the Borg; Heidegger's fear of passivity).

sections.title: Embodied Design Practice (opening)
sections.summary: Sketches embodied, non-dualist methods; design thinking's human-centeredness; Krippendorff's semantic turn (meaning matters; making 'homes'); the systemic turn (service/speculative-critical design; product vs. service vs. experience design); situated design (Brereton; context as enacted, Suchman/Dourish); Dourish's embodied interaction; ethnography / design ethnography; context and the emergence of meaning; need to shed Cartesian/positivist baggage.

key_terms.gloss: Thinking is embodied in the world; we do not build theoretical models and then act on them but interact with things and learn, shaping future behavior. Acknowledges context, experience, and praxis.
The disembodied designer-assumptions Wendt clears: (1) users are rational subjects; (2) users are conscious of their own goals; (3) users think-then-act (identify goal, plan, execute).
Merleau-Ponty: the body is neither subject nor object; perception of external reality comes through and in relation to a sense of the body, so a theory of the body is already a theory of perception.

Merleau-Ponty (anti-representational): acquired skills are stored not as mental representations but as solicitations of situations in the world; the learner is presented with 'more and more finely discriminated situations'.

Merleau-Ponty: the body that counts for orientation is not the objective thing in space but 'a virtual body' whose phenomenal place is defined by task and situation - 'my body is wherever there is something to be done'.
The mind's function is not contained in the head but extends into the world (hard drives, phones, maps), while still connected to the body; memory stores are external and accessed through the body.

Bonsiepe: design attaches artifacts to the human body; a tool taken literally as an appendage (mobile phone as extension of the brain, as the hand-axe extends the hand). The action itself creates the coupling.
Ihde: technologies that enable also obscure; the telescope shows the far but hides the near; the same holds for digital technology.
Use of an object's affordances beyond its script (sliding down a handrail); enabled or hindered by embodiment, which limits the possibilities objects afford; tied to objects' 'for-ness' (Franssen).
Latour: an intended/planned action or purpose embedded in an object (speed bump scripts car-slowing); designers embed scripts by making affordances clear.

Gibson (via Norman): perceived possibility for action; objects are perceived first according to their possible actions, not as named things; 'neither objective nor subjective property... both physical and psychical, yet neither'; pure potentiality that communicates and enables action.

Tonkinwise: an affordance is a 'promised action opportunity', utterly unsemiotic - a direct communication 'between things and my body without the involvement of my mind'; Wendt: it forces the user to think what an object CAN DO (abduction toward future use).

Heidegger (Zuhandenheit / Vorhandenheit): the object-in-use recedes into the background (ready-to-hand); the detached, observed object is present-at-hand. Gibson's tool-in-use/tool-detached maps onto this; the interface and affordance shift between the two with the goal.

Meaning arises from the ways we engage with and act within the world; highly personal yet distributed in the environment and contingent on interaction; a brain in a vat would have no meaning despite storing facts.

Krippendorff: study of how designed objects participate in human affairs and support understanding/practice; optimizes meaningfulness, motivation, and human-centeredness by users' own criteria rather than externally measured performance.

Krippendorff: something makes SENSE when we grasp its role in a particular context (one use case); the MEANING of an object is the sum total of all contexts for which someone can imagine some sense for it (a system of sensemaking). Meaning depends on abduction.

Design is related to declarative statements: it does not describe but produces a reality (as declaring a meeting open); 'form expresses a function' declares that an object is there for a purpose, made by a language community with standard practices.

The point of sensemaking and structural coupling between user and object and context; etymologically 'between' + 'face'; an active mediation point and 'generative friction' between formats, not a passive connection.
Hookway: a relation coupling holding-apart and drawing-together, confining and opening, that produces a united condition; Wendt reads an emergent 'third entity': user, system, and user-system.

An invisible object cannot enter awareness without a mediating aid (microscopic life); a transparent object is perceived THROUGH (a window) and can move in and out of awareness unaided. Transparency is more attainable and preferable as a design goal.

key_terms.term: transparency of use vs. transparency of context
key_terms.gloss: Use-transparency = perceptual 'neutrality', technology as a perspicuous interface between humans and world; context-transparency = the cognitive awareness of the mediating role technologies play.

Heidegger (via ch.2): everyday Dasein is one of coping - adapting to environmental influences; a more accurate (and harder) frame for product success than 'invisibility'/'intuition', supported by rapid prototyping and testing.

Ihde: a contradictory wish for total transparency (technology 'becomes me', = no technology) AND for the power/transformation the technology gives; the call for invisible interfaces harbors complete bodily/cognitive incorporation (the Borg).

A technology's capacity to be many things across contexts/goals; the kettle's spout becomes a scratching tool. Designing within multistability means designing for beneficial outcomes rather than dictating one use.

Krippendorff: a shift from humans adapting to technology toward humans influencing technological development, and from pure usability toward supporting diverse practices of living and 'feeling at home' - the acknowledgement that meaning matters.

An extension of the semantic turn (service design, speculative/critical design) toward systemic thinking - the blend of interfaces and cultural-semiotic systems; methods that zoom from macro service ecologies to micro product interfaces.

Brereton: design where understanding/constructing the situation is core; creative research into the situated problem space, with theory deriving from design investigation; context is 'actively produced, maintained and enacted'.

Dourish: an approach to the design and analysis of interaction that takes embodiment to be central to, even constitutive of, the whole phenomenon; lets users negotiate and evolve systems of practice and meaning in the course of interaction.

claims.text: Three Cartesian assumptions pervade design (users are rational subjects; users are conscious of their goals; users think-then-act); the deliverables built on them (flow diagrams, personas, scenarios) are necessary but, unrecognized as disembodied, lead designers down an unnecessarily dualist path.

Thinking is embodied: we do not formulate theoretical models and then act on them but interact with things and learn, shaping future behavior; real understanding comes from acting out what we know, not rote memorization. Knowledge classifies; understanding shows how to use.

Dreyfus's critique of symbolic AI is really a theory of embodied, contextual, praxis-based cognition: humans are bound within their context, and situational elements affect behavior and cognition more than recitable facts (a computer had no bodily experience and could not adapt).

The body is neither subject nor object but an ambiguous third party; perception of external reality comes through a sense of the body, so a theory of the body is already a theory of perception (Merleau-Ponty).

Acquired skills are stored not as mental representations but as the solicitations of situations in the world; much of memory is external to the mind and accessed through the body (Merleau-Ponty; extended mind).

What counts for orientation is the body as 'a system of possible actions, a virtual body' whose place is defined by task and situation - 'my body is wherever there is something to be done'; this raises the design question of guiding conscious and non-conscious goals within multistability.

Making sense of things depends less on what they objectively ARE and more on what they can DO; there is a difference between what content IS and what it allows users to do (organize by user action, not taxonomy).

Experience is the 'earthy' site where body and mind come together: the individual mediates between which actions are possible and which preferable, reading cues from environment and body; bodily capacity limits the hands and thus limits creative misuse.

Affordance theory runs deeper than communication: we perceive objects according to their possible actions before we name them, so affordances frame objects by what they DO, not by what they are; the name is arbitrary relative to function (Gibson).

An affordance is neither an objective nor a subjective property (or both, or neither): it cuts across the subjective-objective dichotomy, is equally a fact of environment and behavior, and points both ways - thus operating outside dualism (Gibson).

Perception of an affordance is near-universal, but the ability to act on it is wholly dependent on bodily capacity; the action itself creates the structural coupling (the handrail affords slideability for both teenager and arthritic elder, but only one can act).

Affordances are utterly unsemiotic - direct communications between things and the body 'without the involvement of my mind' - and amount to forced abductive thinking about what an object CAN DO rather than what exists now (Tonkinwise).

Because affordances resist objective/subjective categories, design can rethink the role of the verb: instead of explaining what objects ARE, articulate what it means for objects TO BE - moving from a metaphysics of design to a phenomenology of design.

Embodied meaning arises from engaging and acting within the world and is distributed in the environment and contingent on interaction; a brain in a vat, despite storing facts, would have no meaning - sensemaking depends on the potential for action.

Meaning is never divorced from context and must be approached from a systems perspective; phenomenology studies the world through the individual's capacity to generate meaning, and that interpretation - finding place between self and world - is experience.

Product semantics should concern not forms/surfaces but the understanding that penetrates them and how artifacts participate in human affairs; it should optimize meaningfulness and human-centeredness by users' own criteria, not externally measured performance (Krippendorff).

Sense and meaning differ by use-context: something makes sense when we grasp its role in one context; meaning is the sum of all contexts for which someone can imagine a sense for it. Experience design's power is fitting individual sense to systemic meaning.

Use is necessary for sensemaking but not necessarily for meaning, which can be distinct from individual sense (we know a tank's meaning without operating one, though it makes little sense to us); Wendt qualifies Krippendorff's 'use is secondary to meaning'.

Language does not merely represent; it does something and creates reality ('I do' at a wedding); communicating is a design activity, and designs released into the world are not simply descriptive - they create new realities.

Design is related to declarative statements: it produces a reality rather than describing one, requiring a mediation between communication/declaration and usability (artwork is pure declaration; designed objects must be usable).

The interface is the point of sensemaking and structural coupling between user and object and context; without interface there are no tools (Bonsiepe), yet it is also a 'generative friction' fitting together things that do not naturally fit.

The interface is a moving concentration of primary and secondary affordances: what counts as the interface is always contextual to the (always shifting) end goal, like the movement between ready-to-hand and present-at-hand.

Bonsiepe's claim that the interface is the designer's 'central domain' is too limiting: it forgets user behaviors and variability and ignores what happens after the interface is designed; fetishizing the interface as the deliverable sustains a dualist illusion and reflects a positivist (Simon) inner/outer model the book rejects.

The interface is an active mediation, not a passive connection: it holds apart and draws together, polices separation while selectively allowing transmission, and produces a united condition - an emergent user-system 'third entity' (Hookway).

'Intuition' and 'invisibility' are inaccurate and potentially harmful design descriptors: they take the unsemiotic nature of affordances too seriously, since almost all interaction calls upon cultural, linguistic, or learned information, making eradication of that information impossible.

Transparency is a more attainable and preferable design goal than invisibility: a transparent object is perceived through and can move in and out of conscious awareness unaided, letting users sustain their relationship with the product even when something goes wrong.

The desire for an invisible interface is contradictory (Ihde's double desire): users want the transformation technology gives while being unaware of its presence; its logical conclusion is complete bodily/cognitive incorporation, validating Heidegger's fear that decreasing interaction-labor yields a docile state in which technology embeds itself into Dasein.

Embodied, non-dualist design proceeds via the semantic turn (meaning matters; designers make 'homes') and a systemic/situated turn: context is actively produced and enacted, designer intention cannot dictate emergent variables, and embodied interaction (Dourish) takes embodiment as constitutive of the whole phenomenon, requiring designers to shed Cartesian/positivist baggage.

interlocutors.name: Maurice Merleau-Ponty
interlocutors.draws: The body as ambiguous third party; 'a theory of the body is already a theory of perception'; skills as solicitations of situations (not representations); the body as a system of possible actions / virtual body. Grounds the chapter's anti-representational, action-oriented embodiment.

interlocutors.name: Andy Clark
interlocutors.draws: Intelligence rooted in 'the tuning of basic responses to a real world'; the 'earthy' realm as the site of cognition. Supplies the cognitive-science warrant for embodiment.

interlocutors.name: Hubert Dreyfus
interlocutors.draws: A Heideggerian demonstration that disembodied, symbolic, rule-based cognition fails because humans are bound within context; AI as the convenient example, not the target.

interlocutors.name: James J. Gibson
interlocutors.draws: Objects perceived according to possible actions before naming; affordance as 'both physical and psychical, yet neither', cutting across the subjective/objective dichotomy. The central dualism-dissolving concept and the by-what-they-do reframe.

interlocutors.name: Don Norman
interlocutors.draws: The working design-practice definition of affordances as elements that communicate possible action (graspability, pushability, sittability); Wendt then deepens it past mere communication.

interlocutors.name: Cameron Tonkinwise
interlocutors.draws: Affordance as 'promised action opportunity', utterly unsemiotic, between things and the body 'without the involvement of my mind'; basis for 'forced abductive thinking'.

interlocutors.name: Klaus Krippendorff
interlocutors.draws: Product semantics; the sense vs. meaning distinction; language games (via Wittgenstein); the semantic turn; interface as 'prototypical artifact of the postindustrial era'. Principal design-theory interlocutor for meaning-formation. (Some claims are qualified/contested.)

interlocutors.name: Gui Bonsiepe
interlocutors.draws: All design 'ends in the body'; structural coupling; 'without interface there are no tools'. Wendt draws structural coupling but CONTESTS his 'interface as central domain' claim.

interlocutors.name: Don Ihde
interlocutors.draws: Amplification/reduction (telescope); embodiment vs. alterity relations; the 'double desire' / paradox of invisibility. Supplies the mediation framework and the contradiction in the invisibility ideal.

interlocutors.name: Bruno Latour
interlocutors.draws: Scripts (intended actions embedded in objects); human/non-human actants behind embodied/ethnographic method.

interlocutors.name: Georg Simmel
interlocutors.draws: The vase handle: design as 'the act of communicating practical use'; the handle's 'reaching out' and connection to human teleology - the pre-Gibson root of affordance-as-communicated-use.

interlocutors.name: Branden Hookway
interlocutors.draws: The most comprehensive definition of the interface as an active relation coupling holding-apart and drawing-together, producing a united user-system condition.

interlocutors.name: Herbert Simon
interlocutors.draws: Artifact as interface between inner and outer environments; named as the POSITIVIST foil the book's post-phenomenological framework rejects.

interlocutors.name: Paul Dourish
interlocutors.draws: Embodied interaction; context as enacted; meaning negotiated and evolved in interaction. The constructive core of embodied design method.

interlocutors.name: Vilem Flusser
interlocutors.draws: The object as 'what gets in the way'; Wendt entertains then QUALIFIES the etymology.

interlocutors.name: Maarten Franssen
interlocutors.draws: Objects have a 'for-ness' that calls forth certain actions, bounded by bodily capacity and opened by creative misuse.

interlocutors.name: Michael May
interlocutors.draws: Humans should rely on designed affordances as animals rely on natural ones; Wendt draws then QUALIFIES the intuition argument.

interlocutors.name: Margot Brereton
interlocutors.draws: Situated design (understanding/constructing the situation is core) vs. the 'conservative' problem-solving model.

interlocutors.name: Martin Heidegger
interlocutors.draws: Readiness-to-hand / presence-at-hand (Zuhandenheit / Vorhandenheit); care; coping; the fear of human passivity before technology. The chapter's ontological frame.

interlocutors.name: Ludwig Wittgenstein
interlocutors.draws: 'Language does not represent, it does something'; appropriateness judged by participants - grounds the performative/creative power of language and design-as-declaration.

design_principles.name: acknowledge disembodied deliverables
design_principles.gloss: Treat flow diagrams, personas, scenarios, and use cases as necessary but inherently disembodied; recognizing this prevents an unnecessarily dualist design path.

design_principles.name: organize by what things DO, not what they ARE
design_principles.gloss: Structure information and labels by user action ('I need to do my taxes') rather than taxonomy ('Taxes > Forms > Individuals').

design_principles.name: design the verb (phenomenology of design)
design_principles.gloss: Design the action an object calls forth rather than the static object; move from articulating what objects ARE to what it means for them TO BE.

design_principles.name: design affordances as potentiality
design_principles.gloss: Create affordances that communicate AND enable action; treat them as pure potentiality and 'forced abductive thinking', not merely visual signals.

design_principles.name: consider affordance with bodily capacity
design_principles.gloss: Account for the gap between perceiving an affordance (near-universal) and being able to act on it (body-dependent); the action creates the coupling.

design_principles.name: fit individual sense to systemic meaning
design_principles.gloss: Design the interaction for immediate sense, then locate that sense within larger systems of meaning / contexts of use.

design_principles.name: mediate declaration and usability
design_principles.gloss: Designed objects must be both declarative (producing a reality, 'there for a purpose') and usable; balance communication/creativity with use.

design_principles.name: treat the interface as active mediation
design_principles.gloss: Design the interface as a moving, active mediation point (and the behaviors/contexts beyond it), not as the 'central domain' or a passive connector.

design_principles.name: pursue transparency, not invisibility/intuition
design_principles.gloss: Aim for a transparent interface that can move in and out of awareness and let users sustain their relationship with the product when something goes wrong, rather than an invisible or 'intuitive' one.

design_principles.name: design for coping, multistability, creative misuse
design_principles.gloss: Use rapid prototyping and continuous testing to design for beneficial outcomes amid multistability and adaptation, rather than dictating a single use.

design_principles.name: adopt situated / embodied-interaction / ethnographic methods
design_principles.gloss: Put context first; treat designer/user/technology/practice as one system; let users negotiate and evolve systems of practice and meaning in interaction.

ro_hooks.hook: 'Solicitations of situations' and 'finely discriminated situations' name a pre-representational taking-of-the-world that maps onto the perception->phantasma moment in the actualization-of-desire chain: the world solicits action before any propositional grasp.

Perceiving objects 'according to their possible actions' BEFORE naming them is a near-isomorph of perception->phantasma->desire: the world disclosed first as action-potential (a kinesis-soliciting appearance), only derivatively as categorized object.

'Meaning arises from engaging and acting within the world' is the design-theoretic counterpart of meaning-formation as the terminus of an embodied perception->action arc: sense-making as the actualization of worldly engagement, not the read-out of an internal representation.

design_lens_relevance: This unit is the embodiment/meaning core of Wendt's design lens. Its yield for the Aristotelian-Heideggerian actualization-of-desire rhetorical ontology is threefold: (1) it supplies a design-native account of the perception->action arc (affordances as action-potential perceived before naming) that parallels the perception->phantasma->desire chain; (2) it reframes meaning-formation as embodied, distributed, and use-contingent (sense vs. meaning), giving the ontology a vocabulary for how a virtual-learning environment forms meaning through situated engagement rather than transmitting representations; (3) its critique of the 'rational, goal-conscious user' and its transparency-over-invisibility proposal give concrete design principles for VLEs that engage non-conscious goals and sustain conscious, coping-capable awareness. The Heideggerian fear that minimizing interaction-labor yields a docile Dasein is directly relevant to assessing engagement vs. captivation in VR/virtual learning.
